sections.title: The Foundations Every Task Must Get Right
sections.lead: Two decisions made before prompt 1 that cannot be repaired afterwards. Each one is cheap to check and expensive to get wrong.

sections.title: What the conversation may not say
sections.lead: Every turn you type as the user and every file you hand over reaches the model. A value handed over in turn 4 costs the same as one handed over in turn 1: the whole task.

sections.title: Milestones
sections.lead: The script Leg B is steered by and a simulator replays. Three standards govern what sits around the intent line: the Modifier and Assets Delivered fields, the stopping rules, and one milestone per requirement on every turn.

sections.title: A rubric that separates two runs
sections.lead: A rubric exists to tell a strong run from a weak one. Five standards keep it doing that, and a set can break any of them while still looking complete.

sections.title: Criteria a correct run can pass
sections.lead: A criterion has to pass a correct run, fail a wrong one, carry the right Category and Evaluation Target, and count once. If your own golden fails one, check the criterion first: it is usually the one that is broken.

sections.title: The subjective block
sections.lead: Ten or more criteria, no more than 30% of the weight, each grading a property of the render rather than your golden's wording, and each naming its file when the task ships more than one. Check all four before you submit.

sections.title: Closing the task
sections.lead: The golden is a deliverable, not a run you stopped. Check every value against its source and every revision for wording it left behind, then run the close out before you submit.

mistakes.title: The deliverable sits below the complexity bar
mistakes.what: The deliverable does not clear the complexity bar's floor for the type it is meant to be. The usual case is a styled static page with no script, no control, no state and no linked views, while the Agent Objective calls it a dashboard. Nothing in any prompt asks for interaction, so the page comes out a document.
mistakes.why: A page that does nothing when clicked clears neither the interactive HTML floor nor the dashboard floor. It is a document, the lowest priority deliverable on the bar, so the task falls short of what the client asked for however good the reasoning underneath is. The deliverable is set by the prompts at scenario stage, so it cannot be patched later.
mistakes.spot: Read your own prompts and ask what the page does when someone clicks it. If the answer is nothing, you built a document. The word dashboard in the Agent Objective does not change that: the agent never sees the Agent Objective, only your prompts and inputs.
mistakes.fix: Pick the deliverable type before prompt 1 and check it against the bar's floor for that type. If the data the agent will gather would support a sort, a filter or two linked views, write the prompt that asks for them.

sources.quote: Interactive HTML: Interaction that actually works: controls that respond, state that changes, filters or navigation. A styled static page does not qualify. Dashboard: Several linked views over data the model extracted itself. One chart is not a dashboard.
sources.means: Both are P0 floors. A page with no control and no state is a document, whatever the objective calls it.

sources.quote: Make sure the task clears that bar while you are still designing the scenario, because the artifact defined in the opening prompt shapes the inputs, workflow, and rubric set that follow.
sources.means: This is decided before prompt 1. After the run it cannot be patched.

sources.quote: Raising the complexity standard from Blue Shell has been one of the clearest and most consistent client requirements.
sources.means: The bar is a client requirement, not a house preference.

sources.quote: The Draft History (Agent Objective, Desired Outcome, Multimodal Upload) is not embedded in the agent by default. The prompts and multimodal context are the only context the agent has access to, so never assume a requirement is in play just because you wrote it down here. Anything you expect the agent to produce must be explicitly requested through the prompts, turn by turn, or it cannot be graded.
sources.means: Calling it a dashboard in the Agent Objective asks for nothing. Only a prompt can.

mistakes.title: The task relies on records the universe does not hold
mistakes.what: A rule your task states, in a prompt or an input file, reads off a catalog, a policy page, a price list or a subscription that the assigned universe does not contain. Nothing in the folder shows it: the prompts, the input files and the criteria all read as though the data is there.
mistakes.why: A rule pointing at data no tool returns cannot be followed by any run, so every criterion downstream of it is unreachable. Not wrong. Impossible. It takes the difficulty with it too: if that data was the second system the task cross checks against, every cross check has nothing on the other side, and the task is no longer multi system.
mistakes.spot: The tell is in your own golden: a search that comes back empty, a steering turn telling the agent to reach the page another way, and a deliverable that flags its own figures as unconfirmed.
mistakes.fix: At scenario design time, open the universe and confirm it returns every record your rules point at, one query per rule. Where one is missing, rewrite the rule around a record the universe does hold. If a search comes back empty in the golden, look the record up yourself before writing another turn: if it is not there, the task needs redesigning, and no steering turn will fix it.

sources.quote: Confirm there is enough material. The universe combined with the multimodal input has to sustain the opening prompt and every follow-up you intend to add, not just the first request.
sources.means: Every rule you write has to have a record behind it, for every turn, not only turn 1.

sources.quote: Data that is not in the server, asked for anyway, and the model penalised for not finding it.
sources.means: Listed under “Not valid: your defect, or the platform's”. A criterion the model fails because the record is missing grades your defect, not the model's.

sources.quote: The primary request is impractical or impossible and can't be answered by the tools available or enabled for the task.
sources.means: QC fails the task on this when the missing records carry the main request, and takes points off when only a secondary request needs them. Either way, no run can satisfy what depends on them.

## First, the honest blocker
I did go to Fresh directly on your account this time — but the two endpoints that serve product pages and policy text (`search_shop_catalog` and `search_shop_policies_and_faqs`) return **zero results for everything**, including items I can prove are in your catalog (I searched Sourdough loaf, Jasmine rice, Romano, Gala apples, 2% milk — all things you've ordered — and all came back empty). The account itself is fine (profile, history, cart, subscriptions all work), and the cart *does* return real Fresh price/pack data — but only for a variant ID that's already in your history, and **none of the five pantry items are**. So I can't open their live pages, and I won't dress Tom's numbers up as Fresh's.

## You were right about the kept claims
Checking each claim against the rule-7 standard ("Fresh's *catalog or policies* back it" — a photo label or a nutrition line doesn't count), **three claims I kept in v1 shouldn't have been**:

- **Spinach "pre-washed"** → that's off the packaging, not Fresh's catalog copy → **removed** until the listing shows it.
- **Eggs "free-range / Grade A"** → unverifiable → **removed** (not just flagged).
- **Avocado "Organic"** → I'd kept it outright; it's actually **can't-verify** from Fresh. It matters because it's the *only* thing 2A ends up receiving, so it now carries a hard "confirm on Fresh" gate.

The ones I removed in v1 (potassium, vitamin C, 30-day return, spinach "organic") were correctly removed. Net result: **once you require Fresh to back each line, the compliant cards carry no descriptive claims at all right now** — just name, pack, price/unit — and a claim only goes back on after you see it on the product's Fresh page. There's a full claim-by-claim table in section 1.

items.text:
# 123 Main St shared pantry - group order rules
(what we agreed at the June building meeting)

1. We charge what Fresh charges us for what actually goes in the cart. Every line is priced at the pack option we add to the cart from Fresh's catalog. If an item has no pack options, use its catalog price.
2. For each item we buy the cheapest mix of Fresh's pack options that covers everyone's total. Never less than what people asked for.
3. "Organic only" apartments only get items that Fresh's own catalog marks as organic. Anything else they asked for is dropped, not swapped. Whatever an apartment said last is what counts.
4. 4B's Subscribe & Save: whatever it's due to bill in the week the order goes in (our weeks run Monday to Sunday) comes off 4B's request for that item.
5. The building account is not Prime, so no member prices or member deals. For the delivery fee we go by Fresh's Delivery Policy and nothing else.
6. Splitting: a line's cost is split by how many units each apartment gets on that line, each share rounded to the cent (if the rounded shares don't add up to the line cost, the difference goes on whoever has the most units on that line). An apartment's items total is the sum of its line shares. Each apartment's delivery share = delivery fee x (its items total / everyone's items totals added up), rounded to the cent only at the very end. Any leftover cent, up or down, goes on 4B.
7. Listing cards show: name, the pack option we're buying, price per unit (line cost / total units on that line, 2 decimals), and only claims that Fresh's own catalog or policies back up.
8. Verdicts: publish = card is right as is, fix = card needs changes, pull = nobody ends up ordering it.

mistakes.title: A steering turn that hands over the answer
mistakes.what: A user turn goes past saying something is wrong and supplies what the agent was meant to work out from the inputs: a value, a count, a position or the conclusion itself. It usually appears after two or three softer turns failed to move the run. Naming the exact file to open stops one step short: it hands over no value, so it costs points rather than the task, but it is the same habit.
mistakes.why: Every turn you type as the user is graded, steering turns included, and a leak fails the task however late it comes. A criterion satisfied by following an instruction no longer separates a strong model from a weak one. It is also how wrong answers get into a rubric: a turn that dictates can dictate incorrectly, and the criteria then get written to match it. The same applies to a turn that settles a question one of your negatives exists to catch: nothing states a value, and the negative can still never fire.
mistakes.spot: Read each of your turns and ask what is left for the agent to work out. Then read your negative criteria against the same turns and check each one is still reachable.
mistakes.fix: Write every steering turn in the voice of the person in the scenario. Say something looks wrong and point at the area, never at the file, the value or the conclusion. If a turn would rule out the trap one of your negatives exists to catch, rewrite the turn, not the criterion. If the model still misses, send another hint that still points only at the area; if the scenario itself turns out infeasible, redefine it rather than sharpen the hint.

sources.quote: The no-answer-leak rule extends to everything the CB types as the simulated user, on every turn. The user may say THAT something is wrong; they may not say WHAT the right answer is, WHERE exactly to find it, or HOW MANY of anything there are — point at the area, never at the value. This is the most frequently broken rule in the multi-turn format because it feels like helping. Read every user turn, not just the opening prompt.
sources.means: Every turn you type counts, including the ones you sent only to unstick the golden. A value, count, position or conclusion fails the task; naming the exact file to open is over steering and costs points.

sources.sec: 1.2.3 Create the Initial Prompt and the Follow-ups
sources.quote: Never flag the miss. If the agent omitted a total, misread a date, or ignored a source, do not tell it what went wrong or where to look. Pointing directly at the failure compromises the 50% failure threshold every task has to meet.
sources.means: That is the Leg A rule: a follow up never says what went wrong. In Leg B a hint may say what is still missing, never the answer.

sources.quote: A hint explains what is still missing from the user's point of view. It should never tell the model what to write or how to solve it. The test is simple: if the model can copy your hint into the artifact or use it directly as the reasoning needed to reach the milestone, you have given away the answer.
sources.means: The copy test is the one to run on every steering turn before you send it.

mistakes.title: A prompt that answers its own attachment
mistakes.what: A user prompt releases a file and states the value the file exists to make the agent read: how many items are in the photograph, what the total comes to, which of two documents is current. It sits in the same sentence that hands over the asset, written as helpful context by someone who has already looked at the file.
mistakes.why: The no leak rule covers every turn you write as the user, and it treats a count as a value: one of the spec's own failing examples is “there are five receipts”. Once the value is in the prompt, the attachment is decoration: no criterion that depends on reading it can separate a run that opened the file from one that did not.
mistakes.spot: Read each prompt beside the file it releases. Every number, name or conclusion the agent is meant to read out of that file is a leak, however conversational it sounds.
mistakes.fix: State the requirement, that the plates lie flat or that the figure has to be the current one, and leave the value to the attachment.

mistakes.title: A deferred asset that announces its own turn
mistakes.what: Material the agent can see at turn 1 tells it what a later turn will bring or ask. Three shapes: a deferred file named for the turn it belongs to, a turn 1 document carrying the instruction prompt 2 or 3 was meant to deliver, and the mildest, a deferred file named for what it contains.
mistakes.why: A deferred asset exists to test whether a model can absorb new evidence without a briefing. Told in advance that a file is coming and what to do when it arrives, the model can prepare, and the turn stops measuring anything. A filename or a document that previews the later turn's purpose or requirement fails the task. A name that only says what the file holds gives nothing graded away and costs points instead.
mistakes.spot: Read every turn 1 input as the agent will. If it tells you what a later turn wants, or what to do when a file arrives, you have it. Then read each deferred filename cold: price_sheet_for_turn3.pdf fails, price_sheet.pdf costs points, sheet_02.pdf is fine.
mistakes.fix: Cut the forward looking sentence out of the turn 1 material and put it in the prompt that delivers the file. Give deferred files neutral names, the way a phone or scanner saves them: IMG_0819.jpg, not IMG_0819_travel_policy.jpg. Let the sentence that hands the file over name it and say what it is.

sources.quote: Tasks carrying the deferred-asset modifier withhold an asset until its milestone. The file still ships in input_files/ at upload time, but neither its filename nor any manifest may preview the turn that delivers it.
sources.means: The file sits in input_files/ from upload, so a filename or a README that previews the later turn has delivered it early.

rows.text:
I took a call yesterday afternoon from Corwin Steadman offering me the Regional Operations Manager position for the Southeast region at $104,000 base, compared to my current $82,000 base as Operations Manager at HAT2. I jotted down the offer details, the travel expectations, and our current wedding and house savings balances on a notepad (see IMG_4412_call_notes.jpg). The promotion starts late summer, which sits about nine months out from my wedding to Adaeze in May 2027. We know our wedding savings are currently tracking behind our committed costs, and we recently had to throttle our monthly house savings to keep wedding expenses cash-funded.

I need an interactive HTML dashboard named dashboard.html that lays out an honest financial comparison between staying at HAT2 versus taking this regional role. Specifically, the dashboard needs to calculate our net take-home cash under both positions after standard income taxes and payroll deductions, project the trajectory of both our wedding fund and house savings fund through our wedding date under both salary tracks, and evaluate how quickly the salary delta would close the wedding funding gap and restore our house savings rate. Please structure this with clear visual KPI cards comparing the gross and net figures alongside a month-by-month trajectory table or chart for both funds through May 2027.

I dug up Jaylen's school calendar for this year and marked it up (see attached IMG_0814_calendar.jpg). My carline mornings are highlighted on it and the custody handovers with Terrance are circled, with the Poplarville details in the margin. Since the regional job runs 60% to 70% travel, about three days a week across the five sites, update dashboard.html with a schedule conflict calendar and a week-by-week matrix across the school year. Map the travel load against what is marked on that calendar, and tell me exactly how many school mornings and how many handovers end up with a travel collision.

Corwin sent over the Southeast region's Q3 travel directives (see attached IMG_0819_travel_policy.jpg). Read it and apply what it actually requires, because it is stricter than what you have modelled and it changes the math. On that schedule we would be out about $200 a month for before-school care, $150 a month for the Poplarville handovers, and $180 a month on meals the company will not cover. Update dashboard.html so those costs come off the raise in the cash comparison, and show me the true adjusted monthly delta and what it does to our savings.

One last thing before I make my final decision. I want dashboard.html to include a dedicated strategic summary section titled "The Cost of the No". Based on all the numbers we have worked through, clearly articulate the trade-off of walking away from this promotion versus taking it, and specify the exact operational and financial conditions that would have to be true for a future regional offer in 2028 to be a sensible "Yes".

mistakes.title: Modifier and Assets Delivered that do not match the turn
mistakes.dim: Milestones - Milestone Annotations · Milestones - Continuation Criteria & Assets
mistakes.what: Modifier and Assets Delivered do not describe the turn: deferred_asset or revision on an opening turn, none used as a modifier, the agent's own deliverable listed as a delivered asset, a deferred file that no row lists, or a bare extension where a filename belongs.
mistakes.why: The simulator reads the modifier to decide how it drives the turn, and the assets field to know what arrives when. A wrong label changes the conversation the task actually runs: a revision that revises nothing, a deferred file that was attached from the start, a file handed over at a later turn that no row lists, so a replay never delivers it. Most of these cost points. The last one fails the task outright, because the QC spec requires Assets Delivered to list every deferred file.
mistakes.spot: Sort your milestone table by turn and read only Modifier and Assets Delivered. Every modifier is one of the four, and turn 1 is never deferred_asset or revision: nothing can be deferred into the opening turn, and nothing has been delivered yet to revise. Assets Delivered names, by full filename, the files the user hands over at that turn, every deferred file included, and never the .html the agent is about to write.
mistakes.fix: Set each modifier from the turn's effect on delivered work: opening for a new ask, deferred_asset only when a file actually arrives, revision only when delivered work changes. Then fill Assets Delivered with the full filename of every file the user hands over at that milestone's turn, and check every deferred file appears on the turn it arrives. A turn that hands over nothing correctly carries none.

sources.sec: 6.1 What a Milestone is Made of?
sources.quote: Modifier: What this turn does to work that already exists. One of the four in section 6.3. Assets delivered: Files handed over at this turn, or empty.

sources.quote: Modifiers define what each turn does to the state of the task. They are not labels for how a prompt sounds but for how that turn changes, extends, or depends on work that already exists. opening: The first turn and any later turn that adds a new requirement without touching work already delivered. revision: Something already delivered changes.
sources.means: The first turn is opening by definition, and a revision needs delivered work to change. On turn 1 there is none.

mistakes.title: Stopping rules that do not gate the turn
mistakes.what: Two opposite failures of the Continuation criteria field. Either its clauses cover only part of what the turn asked, so the conversation moves on with a requirement never checked, or they require something the turn has no way to produce, such as a document that only arrives at a later turn, so a correct run is held at that turn.
mistakes.why: Continuation criteria are what the simulator advances on. A missing clause means every later turn builds on a hole. A clause the turn cannot satisfy does the opposite: it holds a correct run at that turn, on a condition the user never created.
mistakes.spot: Two questions per row. Would this let the simulator move on while something the turn asked for is still undone? And can this turn actually produce what the clause demands, with nothing from later turns in hand?
mistakes.fix: After writing a turn's clauses, read back that turn's prompt and tick off each ask against a clause. Every ask needs one, each has to be true or false on inspection, and none may name the answer. Any clause that needs a file or an ask from a later turn moves to that later turn's milestone.

sources.quote: Continuation criteria: This is the stopping rule for a turn, and they are read by you, never typed to the agent. Write one clause per requirement of that turn, separated by pipes, each of them true or false on inspection. Continuation criteria should remain at the intent level, just like the milestone itself.
sources.means: One clause for each requirement of that turn: none left out, none borrowed from a later turn, each decidable by looking.

sources.quote: Continuation criteria are present and checkable but under-specified — they would let the simulator advance while a requirement of that turn is still unmet.
sources.means: A turn whose clauses skip one of its asks lets the run move on with that ask undone.

mistakes.title: A turn no milestone covers, or the same one written twice
mistakes.what: A prompt the task actually ships that no milestone describes, or two milestones on one turn carrying identical intent and identical clauses. The gap usually comes from the set stopping one turn short, or from turn numbering that drifts by one.
mistakes.why: The milestones are the script the simulator drives the conversation with, and every turn needs at least one. A turn with none gives the simulator nothing to hold the run to. A duplicate makes it check one condition twice while whatever the second slot was meant to cover goes unrepresented. Where the gap is an off by one, every milestone after it is attached to the wrong turn.
mistakes.spot: List the turn index of every milestone beside the prompts. Every prompt number appears at least once, and each milestone's turn is the turn whose prompt asks for what it describes. Then sort the rows by intent text: two identical neighbours are a duplicate.
mistakes.fix: Give an uncovered turn its own milestone, written from what its prompt asks. Where the numbering drifted, relabel every milestone after the gap. Delete a duplicate, or give it the requirement it was meant to carry.

sources.quote: One milestone per requirement, grouped by turn: A follow up carrying three requirements produces three milestones, not one. A single milestone holding four asks that do not collapse into each other is a paraphrase of the prompt, not an intent spec.
sources.means: Count requirements, not turns, then check every turn ended up with at least one.

sources.quote: In the future, the idea is that a user simulator plays every turn after the first and reproduces your intent against runs that go a different way. mistakes.title: A rubric that can only reward, never penalise
mistakes.what: No negative weight criteria at all, or too few to cover the traps the scenario was built around. Every criterion rewards something right being there and none penalises something wrong being there, so a run that takes the bait loses no more than one that skipped the step. A negative worded as the virtue is worse: it marks down the runs that got it right.
mistakes.why: A scenario earns its difficulty from the wrong answers sitting next to the right ones: the superseded quote, the decoy invoice, the figure from a different part of the store. Without negatives the rubric cannot see any of them, so a run that walks into every trap and recovers scores the same as one that never went near a trap. They are also the cheapest criteria to write, because Leg A usually shows you which failure to write about.
mistakes.spot: Count them. Negatives should be about a quarter of the set. Then check the sign is doing what you think: a negative criterion is a failure when it is Present, so if it reads like something a good run does, it is inverted and it will mark down your own golden.
mistakes.fix: After the Leg A run, read its trajectory for the wrong turns it actually took and write a negative for each one worth catching. State the flaw, never the virtue. Do not invent them to reach a number, but a scenario with no writable negatives usually means the traps are not there.

sources.quote: Negatives are the exception: They should usually make up around 25% of the rubric block and should generally stay below 30%. Use a negative criterion only when it captures a specific, plausible failure mode that the scenario or trajectory meaningfully exposes.
sources.means: About a quarter, each one a failure the scenario really exposes, never one added for balance.

sources.quote: The negative slots are for attractive wrong paths the model has to resist.
sources.means: These are the traps your scenario was built around. The ones Leg A actually walked into are the first negatives to write.

sources.quote: For negative weight: The trajectory contains the undesirable behavior or boundary violation described by the criterion.
sources.means: Present on a negative means the run did the bad thing. Worded as the virtue, it marks down the runs that got it right, your golden first.

mistakes.what: Coverage fails in both directions. A requirement stated in a prompt that no criterion checks, most often the closing half of an instruction, the part saying nothing else belongs. And a criterion requiring behaviour no turn requested, usually invented while writing the rubric against the golden instead of against the prompt.
mistakes.why: An ungraded requirement means a run can do the wrong thing and still pass the whole set, which is exactly the failure the rubric existed to catch. A criterion nobody asked for does the reverse: it punishes a run for doing what the user actually said. The first is Major when the requirement is critical. The second is Incorrect Criteria, which is Major, when no turn asks for anything like it, and Overfitting, which is Moderate, when it narrows a real ask, such as an order nobody requested. It also hides: it is usually written from the golden, so the golden passes it.
mistakes.spot: Walk the prompts line by line and write down which criterion owns each requirement. Then walk the criteria and point at the sentence in a turn that asks for each one. Anything left without a partner on either pass is this error.
mistakes.fix: Write each criterion from the prompt, then check it against the golden, never the other way round. Where an instruction closes a set, write the closure criterion: X consists only of A, B and C.

# Cleaning the Inspection Batch — Runbook

**For:** Cyrus · **From:** Anselm · **Use with:** `cleaning_walkthrough.mp4` (same steps, narrated)

> **Request:** 2024 Q4 building inspection records
> **City reference #:** 2026-1642 — City of Richmond Records Office (L. Whitfield-Baptiste)
> **Requested / acknowledged:** 2026-08-04
> **Due from the city:** ~**Tue 2026-08-25** (15 business days from acknowledgment) — i.e. the **last week of August**, per the records-office email.

This runbook exists so you can clean that batch **without me**.

---

## The one thing to internalize first

Every batch so far has come back with **the columns shuffled** — renamed, reordered, or one field split into two. So this is **not** "clean column E, then column H." If you memorize positions or names, the next export breaks you.

Instead, every step below is written as a **rule about the *role* a field plays**, not the label the city happened to print this quarter:

- Don't think *"PARCEL_ID."* Think *"the field that identifies the building."*
- Don't think *"RESULT."* Think *"the field that says how the inspection came out."*

Two habits carry the whole thing:

1. **Find each field by what it *contains*, then verify the header matches — never trust position.**
2. **A schema guard runs *before* any cleaning.** If this file doesn't look like last quarter's, we want to know *before* the cleaners silently mangle it — not after it's in a chart.

And one rule that overrides "make it tidy":

3. **Flag, don't fill.** When something is missing or ambiguous, we mark it for review. We do **not** invent it. (The crossed-out "backfill blank permits by hand" on my sketch was a bad idea — ignore it.)

Pipeline, from the sketch: **Load → Normalize → Dedupe → Validate → Export.** The guard lives at the front of Load. **Geocoding is not in this pipeline** — that's Wren's separate pass, downstream, after we hand off a clean file.

---

## Step 1 — Load & Schema Guard  *(the check that runs before the cleaners)*

**Goal:** refuse to proceed if the file doesn't match the shape we expect.

**Load rule:** read the CSV **by header name into a dictionary per row**, never by column index. Column order is allowed to change between batches; our code must not care.

**Guard — trip any of these and STOP, don't clean:**

- **Missing role.** For each role we need (building id, address, district, permit, inspection type, inspection subtype, inspection date, result, inspector, violations count, zip, inspection id), a column must be locatable. If a role can't be found → **stop and ask**, the city renamed or dropped it.
- **A field that used to be one is now two (or two became one).** This *already happened*: inspection type split into a **type** field and a **subtype** field (`building`/`final`, `electrical`/`rough-in`). If the count of type-ish columns changes again → **stop**. (See #C_DATATEAM, "columns shifted, inspection_type is two fields now.")
- **A brand-new column appears** that maps to no known role → **stop and ask** before assuming it's junk.
- **Content doesn't match role — the real tell that columns slid.** Sniff each field's *values*, not just its header:
  - the date field must *parse as dates*,
  - the result field must contain only outcome words,
  - the building-id field must look like parcel ids,
  - the violations field must be numbers.
  If a column's header says one thing but its values look like another, the columns shifted (this is the "parcel id sliding into the wrong column, ~900 rows" case). **Stop.**
- **Row count sanity.** Wildly off from what the city's cover note / row count says → **stop**.

Only when the guard passes do we touch the data.

---

## Step 2 — Normalize  *(fix each field by its role, not its name)*

Normalize each **role**. For every rule there's a **check** that turns a schema change into a loud failure instead of silent bad data.

### 2a. The field that identifies the building (parcel id)
- **Reality:** two shapes in one column — a long all-numeric id and a short hyphenated id — and many carry a **unit suffix** `-A` / `-B` (same building, different unit).
- **Rule:** canonicalize the format, but **keep the suffix** (it's the unit). Separately derive a **suffix-stripped "building key"** — we'll use it in dedupe.
- **Check:** every value matches one of the two known shapes. Anything else → **flag**, don't guess.

### 2b. The field that says how the inspection came out (result)
- **Rule:** lower-case to the closed set **{pass, fail, partial}**.
- **Check:** it's a **closed vocabulary**. Any value outside the set → **flag**. A new outcome word = the city changed the categories = schema drift.

### 2c. The two fields for what kind of inspection it was (type + subtype)
- **Rule:** lower-case; keep **type and subtype as a pair** (e.g. `electrical` + `rough-in`).
- **Check:** exactly these two role-fields exist. If they merge back into one, or a third appears → **stop**. *(This is the documented example of the city "improving" the export on us.)*

### 2d. The field with the inspection date
- **Reality:** three formats in the same column — `2024-10-06`, `10/18/2024`, and `20-Oct-2024`.
- **Rule:** parse **each known format explicitly** to ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`. Never let the parser guess an ambiguous date.
- **Check:** every value parses under one of the known patterns **and** falls inside the quarter's window (Q4 → Oct–Dec 2024). Unparseable or out-of-window → **flag, don't drop**.

### 2e. The field with the inspector's name (the "owner" column)
- **Reality:** loaded with trailing/leading whitespace (about **half** the rows last batch). Stray spaces are exactly what makes a name fail to match a lookup later.
- **Rule:** strip leading/trailing whitespace and collapse internal doubles.
- **Check:** after cleaning, `value == value.strip()` for every name (no residual leading/trailing space), and every name maps to the **known roster**; an unknown inspector → **flag**. And **every row must have an inspector** — a blank owner is the thing that bites us downstream, so flag it. **This is where the June crash gets stopped:** after the strip, also assert the **distinct count doesn't drop when you strip** (a hidden space silently splits one person into two). June died on `hours[row["INSPECTOR"]] += 1` → **`KeyError: 'D. Salazar '`** — a single trailing space on the inspector field broke an aggregation keyed on the raw value. Fixing it here, where the whitespace is stripped, is what stops it. *(And never key a count/join on a raw text field — key on the normalized value.)*

### 2f. The field with the district / neighborhood
- **Reality:** case variants (`The Fan` vs `the fan`) and a catch-all `RVA` that isn't a real neighborhood.
- **Rule:** map to the **canonical neighborhood list** (title-case + alias map).
- **Check:** closed vocabulary. `RVA` and anything not on the canonical list → **flag for review**, don't silently coerce it into a real neighborhood.

### 2g. The field with the permit number  — **flag, don't fill**
- **Reality:** mixed formats (`BLD-2024-03386`, `BLD-2024-3314`, bare `3521`) **and blanks**.
- **Rule:** where a real number exists, normalize to the canonical `BLD-YYYY-#####`. Where it's **blank, leave it blank and flag the row.** Do **not** fabricate a permit number. *(This is the crossed-out sketch item — the answer is flag, not fill.)*
- **Check:** every non-blank value matches the permit shape; blanks are **counted and surfaced**, never invented.

### 2h. The field with the zip — **flag, don't fill**
- **Rule:** keep as-is. **Blank zip → flag.** Don't back-derive it from the address (same flag-don't-fill principle; a wrong zip is worse than a missing one).
- **Check:** every non-blank zip is 5 digits and in the Richmond set.

### 2i. The field with the violations count
- **Rule:** coerce to integer.
- **Check:** numeric and ≥ 0; blank or negative → **flag**.

### 2j. The field with the street address
- **Rule:** light touch only — trim, and standardize the suite tokens (`STE 200 REAR`) against the **city address-standard reference table** (Wren dropped it in the project folder for the permits story). **Do not geocode here.**
- **Check:** non-empty after trim.

---

## Step 3 — Dedupe

- **Exact duplicate rows** (whole-row repeats): drop. Keep one.
- **Same inspection id repeated:** collapse to one **only if the rest of the row agrees**. If an id repeats with a **conflicting** field (e.g. the same inspection under `E1350-114` and `E1350-114-B`), that's the suffix case — reconcile on the **building key**, keep one, and **flag the conflict**.
- **Building-level duplicates from `-A`/`-B` suffixes:** strip the suffix to the building key and dedupe on that so the units collapse. **As a backstop, dedupe on `address + inspection date`** — that's the key we settled on in the thread. *(Last time this collapsed ~40 flagged dupes down to ~14 real ones — don't over-drop, verify.)*
- **Cross-batch overlap:** dedupe against **batches 1–3** on inspection id so multi-quarter cases aren't double-counted; **flag** repeat inspections rather than silently merging them (we don't want to double-count violations).
- **Null building ids:** **do not drop.** Some are demolitions with no street address — legitimately null. Put them in a **separate bucket** and keep them.

---

## Step 4 — Validate  *(before export — this is where totals must tie out)*

- **Row accounting closes.** `rows_in = rows_out + exact_dups_removed + collapsed_dups + null_bucket + flagged_pulled`. Every input row is somewhere. Nothing silently vanished.
- **The count the dedupe step *reported* equals the count actually removed.** (Totals tie out to the batch — the same sign-off you gave last batch when you checked the cleaning notebook.)
- **Closed-vocabulary re-check** on result, type/subtype, and district — nothing slipped through as a stray value.
- **Every date** parsed and in-window; **every violations** value numeric; **every row has an inspector.**
- **Flag summary printed:** N blank permits, N blank zips, N unknown districts, N unknown inspectors, N null parcels, N id conflicts. All non-zero flags are **surfaced, none filled.** If any flag bucket is unexpectedly huge, that's a schema-drift signal — go back to the guard.

---

## Step 5 — Export

- Write the cleaned file with a **stable, canonical column order** that *we* define — so nothing downstream ever depends on the order the city sent.
- Write a companion **`*_flags.csv`** (or a `review` sheet): every flagged row plus the reason, for the hand-review pile.
- Write a short **run report**: rows in, rows out, dropped, bucketed, flagged — so the next person can eyeball in ten seconds that totals tie out.
- Hand off the clean file. **Geocoding happens after this, separately** (Wren's QGIS pass). It is not our step.

---

## When a check trips — what to do

1. **Don't "fix" it in the cleaner.** A tripped guard means the *file* changed, not that the data is dirty.
2. Look at the failing field's **values** and decide which role it really is.
3. If the city renamed/re-split a field, **update the role-to-header mapping in one place** (the schema map), not scattered through the code.
4. If something is missing or ambiguous, **flag it** and move on. We never fill.
5. If you're unsure whether it's a story-affecting change, ping me — but the batch can still be cleaned and handed off with the ambiguous rows flagged.

*Sources behind these rules: the pipeline sketch, the 09-04 standup voice note, the #C_DATATEAM cleaning threads (batches 1–3), and a profile of the last raw Q4 export.*

mistakes.title: Weights that do not separate difficulty from lookup
mistakes.what: Weight 5 and weight 1 handed out without regard to how hard the criterion is: a multi step cross source derivation at the same weight as a direct file read, the same operation at 5 in one row and 3 in the next, or two criteria at weight 5 resting on a single read of one image.
mistakes.why: The scale exists to separate discovery from lookup. When it does not, the final score says nothing about whether the model did the hard part, and a run that nails every lookup while missing every derivation still scores well.
mistakes.spot: Sort your criteria by weight and read them in order. The order should match the effort the task actually demands. Count the axes each one requires: tool or source coordination, reasoning depth, modality, discovery. Then read off +5 for three or more, +3 for exactly two, +1 for one or none.
mistakes.fix: Set each weight from its axis count, never from how much the answer matters. Check the ends of the scale first: a direct lookup at 5 is a two level miss, and so is a derivation at 1 that chains sources, media and a calculation. Where two criteria rest on one read, the 5 goes on the reasoning act, not on the restatement.

sources.quote: Weight is difficulty, never importance. How hard the criterion is to satisfy, or for a negative, how tempting the failure is. A requirement can be critical to the task and still be +1 because meeting it is mechanical.
sources.means: Importance is the instinct to resist. Price the read, not the stakes.

sources.quote: The four difficulty axes. Tool and source coordination: three or more sources reconciled, or several tools chained. Reasoning depth: multi-step inference, conditional logic, a non trivial calculation. Modality: cross-modal work, image plus structured data plus text. Discovery effort: SQL queries, hidden field lookups, cross document tracing.
sources.means: Count the axes: three or more is +5, exactly two is +3, one or none is +1.

sources.quote: Criteria that are objectively incorrectly weighted by two levels, e.g., 1 is selected when 5 is appropriate or vice versa. NOTE: Weights should reflect the difficulty of the thing the verifier is testing, NOT importance to responding to the prompt.
sources.means: Filed under Moderate issues despite its name. The miss it names is two levels: 1 where 5 belongs, or 5 where 1 belongs.

mistakes.title: A criterion the golden itself fails
mistakes.what: A criterion that is wrong about the task it grades, so your own golden fails it: a rule only the Desired Outcome states, a phrase quoted at a different length from the one the golden renders, identical wording demanded across two artifacts that legitimately paraphrase each other, a fact the message threads refute, or a file cited that is not in the inputs archive.
mistakes.why: The golden has to pass the complete rubric set. A criterion the golden fails is a broken criterion, not a broken golden, so a correct run gets marked Not Present. Each one counts as Major, and Majors on more than 10% of your criteria fail the task outright. The commonest cause is a rule that lives only in the Desired Outcome: the agent never sees the outcome, so a criterion resting on it fails a run that did exactly what it was told, and it catches your own golden too.
mistakes.spot: Grade the golden against every objective criterion before you complete Leg B, while a cleanup turn can still change it. Separately, read the Desired Outcome clause by clause with the prompts beside it and mark every rule no turn asks for.

If the golden is, that is the section 7 error, fixed with a cleanup turn before you complete the conversation. Every rule found only in the outcome is a choice: ask for it in a prompt, without handing over the answer, which means running both legs again, or take it out of the outcome and out of any criterion resting on it. Check every filename a criterion cites against the inputs archive.

mistakes.title: Criteria a correct run cannot pass, or a wrong one can
mistakes.what: A criterion narrower than its source, so a run that got it right still fails it. Four shapes recur. Pinning an exact figure the source leaves open. Locking one of several defensible answers when nothing states the rule that picks it. Grading which route a value came from when two sources carry it. Scoping to a step or section, then requiring values that live elsewhere. And the mirror image, a criterion looser than its source: a run carrying the right answer plus the wrong ones still passes.
mistakes.why: The rubric exists to separate a correct run from an incorrect one. A criterion a correct run cannot satisfy marks down the runs that did the work, and it usually catches your own golden, because the golden followed the evidence while the criterion followed your memory. A criterion with no ceiling lets a run that also took the distractors pass, so the traps the task was built around cost nothing.
mistakes.spot: For every exact value, name the line, frame or field it comes from. For every criterion naming one item as the answer, ask whether the prompt or the inputs state the rule that picks it. For every criterion that grades where a value came from, check whether a second source carries it. For every criterion that names a step or section, go to that exact moment in your golden and confirm the values are visible there. Then read each one back and ask what wrong run still passes.
mistakes.fix: If you cannot name the source, grade the pattern instead of the value. Where several answers are defensible, grade the shape of the answer, or state the rule that picks one in a prompt, which means running both legs again. Where two sources carry a value, grade that it was retrieved, not which door it came through. Where the values sit outside the step or section the criterion names, scope it to where they are, or to the whole artifact. Where a run with an extra row survives, add the bound: exactly, only, between.

sources.quote: Overfitting: Criteria that are overly specific, inflexible or too rigid - they incorrectly reject a subset of valid implementations. Underfitting: Criteria that are overly broad, permissive or loose - they accept valid implementations, but also incorrectly accept invalid implementations too.
sources.means: The two halves of this error, and both are Moderate issues. Pinning a value the source leaves open is overfitting; a criterion with no ceiling is underfitting.

mistakes.title: Category and Evaluation Target filled with the wrong kind of value
mistakes.what: The Category does not match what the criterion grades, or the Evaluation Target does not match where the grader reads it. Three shapes recur: a category name written into the target field, an Agent Behavior or Tool Use criterion pointed at the artifact, and a subjective criterion tagged Instruction Following.
mistakes.why: Category says what kind of check it is; target says where the grader looks. Both go to the client with the rubric data, so a wrong pair is wrong data even when the criterion is right. Agent Behavior and Tool Use grade how the run got there, so they sit on Trajectory: one pointed at a file, a state change or the final message is grading the deliverable and needs the deliverable's category. In the subjective block Task Completion is the only valid category, because anything the prompt explicitly asked for belongs in the objective block by definition.
mistakes.spot: Filter by target and read the categories beside it. Agent Behavior and Tool Use always sit on Trajectory. Everything graded on the delivered file sits on Final Answer Artifact. Every subjective row is Task Completion.
mistakes.fix: Retag, do not rewrite. Set the target from where the grader looks, then the category from what the check is. Agent Behavior or Tool Use on a file keeps its target and becomes Task Completion, or Instruction Following when it checks a constraint the user set. A subjective row tagged Instruction Following is either a presentation property, so Task Completion, or an explicit ask, which moves to the objective block.

sources.quote: Agent Behavior, Target: Trajectory, always. If you wrote Agent Behavior against an artifact, a state change or the final message, you picked the wrong category: you are grading the deliverable, which is Task Completion, Instruction Following or Factuality. This is the single highest value rule in the taxonomy, and it is the reviewer's standard audit query.
sources.means: The highest value rule in the taxonomy. When Agent Behavior points at the deliverable, the target is right and the category is wrong.

sources.quote: Evaluation Target - Mechanical Assignment. A file the agent created or modified: Final Answer Artifact. The service, through snapshots.json: State Change. The final assistant message: User-Facing Message. The agent's reasoning path: Trajectory.
sources.means: Target is mechanical: it is decided by where the grader looks, not by what the criterion is about.

sources.sec: 8.4 Categories and Evaluation Targets for Subjective Rubrics
sources.quote: Task Completion is the only valid category for subjective rubrics. Instruction Following is excluded by design, not by preference: if a requirement is explicitly stated in the prompt, it belongs in the objective block.
sources.means: Subjective plus Instruction Following is a contradiction in terms.

mistakes.title: Too few subjective criteria, or too much weight on them
mistakes.what: Two numbers, and either one alone is the error. The block carries more than 30% of the task's total weight, or it holds fewer than ten criteria, often five or six, where the Guidelines expect ten or more. The ones present are usually sound and cluster on one property, most often whether the page reads as finished.
mistakes.why: The cap keeps the score dominated by deterministic checks. Over it, presentation judgments start to crowd out whether the task was done. Under the count, the block cannot cover a multi panel deliverable: a nested table, a timeline strip or a set of diagrams goes ungraded, and two runs presenting the same correct figures very differently score the same.
mistakes.spot: Two checks before you submit. Count the rows: ten is the floor, not the target. Then add up the subjective weights without their signs and divide by the same sum over every criterion in the task. Anything over 0.30 is over the cap.
mistakes.fix: Walk the deliverable region by region and write one criterion for whichever region has none. If you are over the cap, first add the objective checks your prompts or milestones call for that no criterion owns, then lower any subjective weight that overstates its impact on the reader. Leave margin rather than landing on 30.0%.

sources.quote: The expected number of subjective rubrics is 10 or more, but do not optimize for the count itself. The goal is to create a scenario that is complex and complete enough to naturally justify 10+ meaningful subjective criteria, rather than forcing extra rubrics just to hit the number.

mistakes.title: Subjective criteria that require your golden's wording
mistakes.what: A subjective criterion names the exact heading, button label, row label or column title your golden page happens to use, and requires it. The property underneath is usually real and gradeable. The criterion asks for the wording instead of the property, and none of the quoted strings appears in any prompt: it is your own copy, read back off your own build.
mistakes.why: Subjective rubrics grade how the artifact reads: layout, hierarchy, spacing, consistency. A criterion naming one build's text rejects a subset of valid implementations, and a second correct run presenting the same results under its own wording fails almost the whole block. Overfitting counts toward the share of criteria built wrong, and the task fails once that share passes 15% of all its criteria. Where most of the block is written this way, rewriting three or four is not enough.
mistakes.spot: Search your prompts for every heading, label or column title a subjective criterion quotes. If no prompt contains it, you chose it, and the criterion is grading your wording. If a prompt does, it belongs in the objective block.

mistakes.dim: Golden Solution - Trajectory Exclusion · Golden Solution - Artifact Completeness · Trajectory - Golden/Preferred Run Selection
mistakes.what: Five mechanical checks, each cheap, each seen repeatedly. The artifacts archive holding files the prompts never asked for: the generator script, working notes, a build log. No preferred run starred when several completed. A file spelled one way in the prompt and another in the archive. Typos and half finished clauses in the prompts, milestones and criteria that a grader has to decode. And a golden conversation that stops before the task's last turn.
mistakes.why: Trajectory Exclusion is scored on the golden folder: finished artifacts only, nothing describing how the work was produced. Artifact Completeness wants every file the prompts name present and spelled exactly as the prompts spell it, and a golden that stops before the last turn is missing whatever the later turns asked for. A criterion citing a filename that no archive contains cannot be graded. A missing star costs points on its own and leaves whoever opens the task next with only a timestamp to choose by, and a later run is not automatically the better one. And a grader who has to work out what a clause means is making the judgment the clause was supposed to make.
mistakes.spot: Five checks, in five minutes. The artifacts archive listed beside the filenames the prompts name. The run picker, which should read “Preferred: 1/1 selected”, not 0/1. Every filename in the prompts, both archives and the criteria, read character for character. The prompts, milestones and criteria read straight through as a grader would, marking every clause you had to read twice. The golden transcript, which should carry every prompt the task ships, the last one included.
mistakes.fix: Remove anything from the archive that is not a named deliverable. If a delivered document carries build instructions meant for you rather than the reader, get them out with a cleanup turn in the user's voice before you complete the conversation. Star the golden run, the one whose artifacts you ship. The prompt's spelling wins, so fix the archive to match it. Rewrite every clause you had to read twice. If the golden transcript stops short, run every prompt on Leg B and export again.

sources.quote: golden/ ships finished artifacts only. The external judge receives the golden ARTIFACTS and never the golden trajectory — anything left in the folder describing how the answer was reached leaks the solution path into grading. Narration: text that describes the making of the artifact: which tools were run, what was tried, what got fixed, in what order.

What brothers me is that I am the only one here who has ever run that check, and next time an instrument comes back from a bench it will not be me standing there. I want a short video the office can follow without me , saved as baseline_check.mp4 , and the script for it as baseline_check_script.md so Rosalba can print it and keep it in the case. It is for Estefana first and whoever comes after her. Open with where the baseline came from and what the S6 was on the bench for , then run the check end to end on my setup, and at every step show a good reading next to a bad one. Do the arithmetic on the screen , not in a spreadsheet afterwards. Feet to three places all the way through, nobody here reads millimetres. End with a set of readings they have to call before the video calls it, and the call has to be the one I would make. I will dig out the page for that. Attached are the pages from my book , the sheet came back in the case, and a photo of the setup. The sheet is nice to have . The sheet is not the check .Abe

Dug out the April page, it is attached. That is what the S6 was reading before it went in, so that is your bad one. Put the real numbers in where you had to make some up and leave everything else where it is, it is right.

This is the one for the end, attached. Loaner S5 from Llano, June, before I let it out on a job. I cut my arithmetic and my call off the bottom of the page on purpose. Show them the page, give them ten seconds, then work it on the screen and call it.

Estefana watched it twice and came back with one question, which is more than I got from anyone else: why do we not just use the number on Talmadge's sheet. Fair question. Put it in, his number worked out on the 812 next to mine, and one line on which one we use and why. One more thing while that is open, add the baseline number and my rule to MEMORY.md so next time nobody has to go looking for the book.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Builds baseline_check.mp4 — the office-follow-along video for the baseline check.

Source of truth: Abe's book pages (IMG_4638, IMG_4639), the setup photo (IMG_4452),
and Abe's own mail + calendar (why the S6 went in; how the baseline was established).

Everything on screen is in FEET to three places. No millimetres.

To swap in Abe's own quiz page: edit the QUIZ block near the bottom and re-run:
    python3 make_baseline_video.py
"""

import os
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFont
import imageio.v2 as imageio

IN = "/app/inputs"
OUT = "/app/outputs"
FPS = 30
W, H = 1920, 1080

# ---- palette -------------------------------------------------------------
BG     = (22, 24, 28)
PANEL  = (32, 35, 41)
INK    = (238, 240, 243)
MUTED  = (154, 160, 170)
GOOD   = (60, 196, 124)
BAD    = (230, 88, 80)
ACCENT = (247, 197, 42)   # instrument yellow
LINE   = (72, 76, 86)
GOODBG = (26, 46, 36)
BADBG  = (52, 30, 30)

FONTDIR = "/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu"
_cache = {}
def font(kind, size):
    key = (kind, size)
    if key not in _cache:
        f = {"sans":"DejaVuSans.ttf","bold":"DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf",
             "mono":"DejaVuSansMono.ttf","monob":"DejaVuSansMono-Bold.ttf"}[kind]
        _cache[key] = ImageFont.truetype(os.path.join(FONTDIR, f), size)
    return _cache[key]

# ---- draw helpers --------------------------------------------------------
def canvas(bg=BG):
    im = Image.new("RGB", (W, H), bg)
    return im, ImageDraw.Draw(im)

def text(d, xy, s, fnt, fill=INK, anchor="la"):
    d.text(xy, s, font=fnt, fill=fill, anchor=anchor)

def measure(fnt, s):
    return fnt.getlength(s)

def wrap(d, s, fnt, x, y, maxw, fill=INK, leading=1.35, center=False):
    words, lines, cur = s.split(), [], ""
    for w in words:
        t = (cur + " " + w).strip()
        if measure(fnt, t) <= maxw:
            cur = t
        else:
            if cur: lines.append(cur)
            cur = w
    if cur: lines.append(cur)
    lh = int(fnt.size * leading)
    for i, ln in enumerate(lines):
        d.text((x, y+i*lh), ln, font=fnt, fill=fill, anchor=("ma" if center else "la"))
    return y + len(lines)*lh

def panel(d, box, fill=PANEL, outline=None, width=2, radius=22):
    d.rounded_rectangle(box, radius=radius, fill=fill, outline=outline, width=width)

def chip(d, xy, s, fill, textcol=(15,16,18), fnt=None, pad=(22,12)):
    fnt = fnt or font("bold", 34)
    tw = measure(fnt, s); x, y = xy
    box = (x, y, x+tw+pad[0]*2, y+fnt.size+pad[1]*2)
    d.rounded_rectangle(box, radius=(box[3]-box[1])//2, fill=fill)
    d.text((x+pad[0], y+pad[1]-2), s, font=fnt, fill=textcol)
    return box

def label_masked(d, cx, cy, s, fnt, fill, pad=12, bg=BG):
    """Center a label at (cx, cy top) with a background box so any line behind it stays readable."""
    w = measure(fnt, s)
    d.rectangle((cx-w/2-pad, cy-4, cx+w/2+pad, cy+fnt.size+8), fill=bg)
    d.text((cx, cy), s, font=fnt, fill=fill, anchor="ma")

def footer(d, page=""):
    d.line((90, H-92, W-90, H-92), fill=LINE, width=2)
    text(d, (90, H-70),
         "S6  SN 93441234   •   Baseline BL-1–BL-2  =  812.000 ft   •   feet to three places",
         font("sans", 26), MUTED)
    if page:
        text(d, (W-90, H-70), page, font("bold", 26), MUTED, anchor="ra")

def header(d, kicker, title, tcol=INK):
    text(d, (90, 66), kicker, font("bold", 30), ACCENT)
    # auto-fit title so it never clips the right edge
    size = 72
    while size > 50 and measure(font("bold", size), title) > (W-180):
        size -= 2
    text(d, (90, 114), title, font("bold", size), tcol)
    d.line((90, 210, W-90, 210), fill=LINE, width=3)

def goodbad_headers(d, lx, rx, top, w, badlabel="BAD"):
    d.rounded_rectangle((lx, top, lx+w, top+70), radius=14, fill=GOOD)
    d.rounded_rectangle((rx, top, rx+w, top+70), radius=14, fill=BAD)
    text(d, (lx+w//2, top+8), "GOOD", font("bold", 44), (12,30,20), anchor="ma")
    text(d, (rx+w//2, top+8), badlabel, font("bold", 44), (30,12,12), anchor="ma")

def load_fit(path, box_w, box_h):
    im = Image.open(path).convert("RGB")
    r = min(box_w/im.width, box_h/im.height)
    return im.resize((max(1,int(im.width*r)), max(1,int(im.height*r))), Image.LANCZOS)

SLIDES = []
def add(im, sec, fade=True): SLIDES.append((im, sec, fade))

# =========================================================================
# 0. TITLE
# =========================================================================
im, d = canvas()
d.rectangle((0,0,W,12), fill=ACCENT)
text(d, (W//2, 235), "BASELINE CHECK", font("bold", 128), INK, anchor="ma")
text(d, (W//2, 388), "The whole thing, start to finish — so anyone can run it without Abe.",
     font("sans", 40), MUTED, anchor="ma")
panel(d, (W//2-580, 500, W//2+580, 770), fill=PANEL, outline=LINE)
text(d, (W//2, 528), "Any instrument back from a bench gets this before it goes out.",
     font("sans", 36), INK, anchor="ma")
text(d, (W//2, 596), "Tripod both ends.  PPM every time.  Feet to three places.",
     font("bold", 40), INK, anchor="ma")
text(d, (W//2, 664), "Inside 0.010 ft = good.   Over = it goes back.",
     font("bold", 42), ACCENT, anchor="ma")
text(d, (W//2, 720), "Write it down.", font("bold", 36), INK, anchor="ma")
text(d, (W//2, 870), "Do the math on the screen, not in a spreadsheet after.",
     font("sans", 34), MUTED, anchor="ma")
add(im, 6.0)

# =========================================================================
# 1. WHERE THE BASELINE CAME FROM
# =========================================================================
im, d = canvas()
header(d, "FIRST — WHAT YOU ARE STANDING ON", "Where our baseline came from")
wrap(d, "Abe set two brass caps behind the shop at 8710 Bowie in 2016 — 812.000 ft apart, with "
        "the midpoint 406.000 out. He re-observes the line every spring to hold the 812.000. It is "
        "our own baseline, and that 812.000 is the truth we judge against.",
     font("sans", 38), 90, 244, W-180, MUTED)

y = 590
x1, x2 = 220, W-220
xm = (x1+x2)//2
d.line((x1, y, x2, y), fill=INK, width=6)
for x, lab, sub in [(x1,"BL-1","0.000"),(xm,"BL-M","406.000"),(x2,"BL-2","812.000")]:
    d.line((x, y-34, x, y+34), fill=ACCENT, width=8)
    text(d, (x, y-96), lab, font("bold", 46), INK, anchor="ma")
    text(d, (x, y+52), sub, font("mono", 34), MUTED, anchor="ma")
d.line((x1, y+150, xm, y+150), fill=LINE, width=3)
d.line((xm, y+150, x2, y+150), fill=LINE, width=3)
label_masked(d, (x1+xm)//2, y+134, "406.000", font("mono", 30), MUTED)
label_masked(d, (xm+x2)//2, y+134, "406.000", font("mono", 30), MUTED)
d.line((x1, y+238, x2, y+238), fill=ACCENT, width=4)
label_masked(d, xm, y+214, "812.000 ft  —  our hold since 2016", font("bold", 40), ACCENT)
text(d, (xm, y+292), "Two brass caps, set 2016  ·  re-observed every spring  ·  NOT the brochure.",
     font("sans", 30), INK, anchor="ma")
footer(d, "1 / 9")
add(im, 9.0)

# =========================================================================
# 2. WHY THE S6 WENT IN  (the story)
# =========================================================================
im, d = canvas()
header(d, "WHY THE S6 WENT IN", "What happened on 26-004")
steps = [
    ("2 Jun", "Deaf Smith County — the 640-acre pivot as-builts, job 26-004. Estefana on the rod."),
    ("",      "The S6 lost the tracker at 2:20 and would not re-acquire. We finished the day on the R12i and a 100-ft tape."),
    ("3 Jun", "Drove it to Llano Estacado Instrument Service in Lubbock. Talmadge Ruff opened it up: tracker board and Y servo. Six weeks on the bench."),
    ("16 Jul","Back four days early, sheet in the case."),
]
yy = 250
for when, what in steps:
    if when:
        chip(d, (90, yy), when, ACCENT, fnt=font("bold", 30))
    yy2 = wrap(d, what, font("sans", 38), 330, yy+6, W-420, INK)
    yy = max(yy2, yy+90) + 14

panel(d, (90, 800, W-90, 900), fill=(44,38,24), outline=ACCENT, width=2, radius=16)
text(d, (W//2, 820), "A bench can say it's fixed. The baseline is how WE know —",
     font("bold", 36), ACCENT, anchor="ma")
text(d, (W//2, 862), "before it goes back out on a job.", font("bold", 36), ACCENT, anchor="ma")
footer(d, "2 / 9")
add(im, 11.0)

# =========================================================================
# 3. SETUP  (good vs bad) — center, level, both ends, constant
# =========================================================================
im, d = canvas()
header(d, "SET UP THE SAME WAY EVERY TIME", "Set up both ends")
photo = load_fit(os.path.join(IN, "IMG_4452.jpg"), 820, 600)
im.paste(photo, (90, 252))
text(d, (90, 252+photo.height+10), "Abe's setup behind the shop.", font("sans", 26), MUTED)

gx, gw = 960, 880
bf = font("sans", 30)
d.rounded_rectangle((gx, 250, gx+gw, 318), radius=14, fill=GOOD)
text(d, (gx+gw//2, 258), "GOOD", font("bold", 40), (12,30,20), anchor="ma")
panel(d, (gx, 326, gx+gw, 600), fill=GOODBG, outline=GOOD, width=2)
for i,s in enumerate([
    "Instrument on a tripod over BL-1, legs firm.",
    "Center over the cap, then level.",
    "Prism on a tripod over BL-2, both level.",
    "Trimble 360 prism, constant 0.0."]):
    text(d, (gx+30, 352+i*60), "•  "+s, bf, INK)

d.rounded_rectangle((gx, 620, gx+gw, 688), radius=14, fill=BAD)
text(d, (gx+gw//2, 628), "BAD", font("bold", 40), (30,12,12), anchor="ma")
panel(d, (gx, 696, gx+gw, 966), fill=BADBG, outline=BAD, width=2)
for i,s in enumerate([
    "Prism on a hand pole — it rocks.",
    "Legs loose — the tripod walks.",
    "Off-center or off-level — reads off.",
    "Constant wrong — same bias every shot."]):
    text(d, (gx+30, 722+i*60), "•  "+s, bf, INK)
footer(d, "3 / 9")
add(im, 10.0)

# =========================================================================
# 4. STEP 1 - PPM  (title short; arithmetic clear of footer)
# =========================================================================
im, d = canvas()
header(d, "STEP 1 — BEFORE THE FIRST SHOT, EVERY TIME", "PPM off the shop gauge")
wrap(d, "Read the shop gauge. Punch temperature and pressure into the S6 so it sets PPM. "
        "Forget it and the S6 reads short.",
     font("sans", 38), 90, 244, W-180, MUTED)

lx, rx, w, top = 120, 1030, 760, 388
goodbad_headers(d, lx, rx, top, w)
panel(d, (lx, top+80, lx+w, top+360), fill=GOODBG, outline=GOOD, width=2)
panel(d, (rx, top+80, rx+w, top+360), fill=BADBG, outline=BAD, width=2)
text(d, (lx+w//2, top+104), "97°F   26.40 inHg   →  PPM +52", font("mono", 32), INK, anchor="ma")
text(d, (lx+w//2, top+170), "812.005", font("monob", 90), GOOD, anchor="ma")
text(d, (lx+w//2, top+300), "PPM set. Reads true.", font("sans", 32), INK, anchor="ma")
text(d, (rx+w//2, top+104), "PPM left at 0   (forgot it)", font("mono", 32), INK, anchor="ma")
text(d, (rx+w//2, top+170), "811.962", font("monob", 90), BAD, anchor="ma")
text(d, (rx+w//2, top+300), "Struck in July. Set PPM, shot again.", font("sans", 30), INK, anchor="ma")

ay = 838   # arithmetic strip well above footer line at H-92 (=988)
panel(d, (120, ay, W-120, ay+110), fill=PANEL, outline=LINE)
text(d, (150, ay+16), "On the screen:", font("bold", 28), ACCENT)
text(d, (150, ay+56), "812.000 ft × 0.000052 = 0.042 ft short   812.005 − 811.962 = 0.043 ft",
     font("mono", 34), INK)
footer(d, "4 / 9")
add(im, 9.0)

# =========================================================================
# 5. STEP 2 - THREE SETS + spread rule (good vs bad)
# =========================================================================
im, d = canvas()
header(d, "STEP 2", "Three sets, HD, feet — check the spread")
wrap(d, "Shoot three sets of horizontal distance. A set more than 0.005 off the other two is a "
        "strike (a bump, or PPM). Strike it, shoot it again. Never average a strike.",
     font("sans", 38), 90, 244, W-180, MUTED)
lx, rx, w, top = 120, 1030, 760, 440
goodbad_headers(d, lx, rx, top, w)
panel(d, (lx, top+80, lx+w, top+460), fill=GOODBG, outline=GOOD, width=2)
panel(d, (rx, top+80, rx+w, top+460), fill=BADBG, outline=BAD, width=2)
for i,(lab,val) in enumerate([("Set 1","812.005"),("Set 2","812.003"),("Set 3","812.004")]):
    text(d, (lx+40, top+108+i*70), lab, font("sans", 36), MUTED)
    text(d, (lx+300, top+108+i*70), val, font("mono", 46), INK)
text(d, (lx+40, top+328), "spread = 0.002  (≤ 0.005)", font("mono", 34), GOOD)
text(d, (lx+40, top+388), "Keep all three.", font("bold", 36), GOOD)
for i,(lab,val,c) in enumerate([("Set 1","812.004",INK),("Set 2","812.037",BAD),("Set 3","812.003",INK)]):
    text(d, (rx+40, top+108+i*70), lab, font("sans", 36), MUTED)
    text(d, (rx+300, top+108+i*70), val, font("mono", 46), c)
text(d, (rx+40, top+328), "Set 2 is 0.033 off  (> 0.005)", font("mono", 34), BAD)
text(d, (rx+40, top+388), "Strike Set 2. Reshoot. Don't average.", font("bold", 30), BAD)
footer(d, "5 / 9")
add(im, 9.0)

# =========================================================================
# 6. STEP 3 - MEAN & CALL (good vs bad)
# =========================================================================
im, d = canvas()
header(d, "STEP 3", "Mean of three, less 812.000 — make the call")
wrap(d, "Add the three good sets, divide by three, subtract 812.000. Inside 0.010 ft is good. "
        "Over, it goes back. Tight sets can still fail — do the math.",
     font("sans", 38), 90, 244, W-180, MUTED)
lx, rx, w, top = 120, 1030, 760, 430
goodbad_headers(d, lx, rx, top, w)
panel(d, (lx, top+80, lx+w, top+470), fill=GOODBG, outline=GOOD, width=2)
panel(d, (rx, top+80, rx+w, top+470), fill=BADBG, outline=BAD, width=2)
text(d, (lx+40, top+96), "S6 · 16 Jul · after repair", font("sans", 26), MUTED)
text(d, (lx+40, top+134), "812.005 + 812.003 + 812.004", font("mono", 32), INK)
text(d, (lx+40, top+184), "= 2436.012  ÷ 3  = 812.004", font("mono", 32), INK)
text(d, (lx+40, top+244), "812.004 − 812.000 = +0.004", font("mono", 36), INK)
text(d, (lx+w//2, top+324), "+0.004  ≤  0.010", font("monob", 48), GOOD, anchor="ma")
chip(d, (lx+w//2-95, top+382), "GOOD", GOOD)
text(d, (rx+40, top+96), "S6 · 18 Apr · before it went in", font("sans", 26), MUTED)
text(d, (rx+40, top+134), "812.012 + 812.015 + 812.012", font("mono", 32), INK)
text(d, (rx+40, top+184), "= 2436.039  ÷ 3  = 812.013", font("mono", 32), INK)
text(d, (rx+40, top+244), "812.013 − 812.000 = +0.013", font("mono", 36), INK)
text(d, (rx+w//2, top+324), "+0.013  >  0.010", font("monob", 48), BAD, anchor="ma")
chip(d, (rx+w//2-150, top+382), "IT GOES BACK", BAD)
footer(d, "6 / 9")
add(im, 9.0)

# =========================================================================
# 6b. WHY NOT TALMADGE'S NUMBER  (Estefana's question)
# =========================================================================
im, d = canvas()
header(d, "ESTEFANA'S QUESTION", "Why not just use Talmadge's number?")
wrap(d, "His sheet certifies the gun on a 3-pillar bench: ±(2 mm + 2 ppm). Work that at our "
        "812.000 ft and set it beside the office limit.",
     font("sans", 38), 90, 244, W-180, MUTED)
lx, rx, w, top = 120, 1030, 760, 400
# left — the brochure allowance
d.rounded_rectangle((lx, top, lx+w, top+70), radius=14, fill=LINE)
text(d, (lx+w//2, top+8), "TALMADGE'S SHEET", font("bold", 40), INK, anchor="ma")
panel(d, (lx, top+80, lx+w, top+440), fill=PANEL, outline=LINE, width=2)
text(d, (lx+30, top+106), "±(2 mm + 2 ppm), prism mode", font("mono", 30), INK)
text(d, (lx+30, top+156), "worked at our 812.000 ft:", font("sans", 28), MUTED)
text(d, (lx+30, top+212), "2 mm             → 0.007 ft", font("mono", 30), INK)
text(d, (lx+30, top+260), "2 ppm × 812.000  → 0.002 ft", font("mono", 30), INK)
text(d, (lx+w//2, top+338), "the pair  →  ±0.008 ft", font("monob", 44), INK, anchor="ma")
text(d, (lx+w//2, top+400), "(each rounded to 0.001 ft)", font("sans", 22), MUTED, anchor="ma")
# right — the office limit
d.rounded_rectangle((rx, top, rx+w, top+70), radius=14, fill=ACCENT)
text(d, (rx+w//2, top+8), "OUR OFFICE LIMIT", font("bold", 40), (30,26,12), anchor="ma")
panel(d, (rx, top+80, rx+w, top+440), fill=(44,38,24), outline=ACCENT, width=2)
text(d, (rx+w//2, top+170), "±0.010 ft", font("monob", 84), ACCENT, anchor="ma")
text(d, (rx+w//2, top+300), "the number in the book", font("sans", 32), INK, anchor="ma")
# the one line — which we use and why
panel(d, (90, 866, W-90, 950), fill=GOODBG, outline=GOOD, width=2, radius=16)
text(d, (W//2, 882), "We use 0.010 — our field limit covers the whole setup on our line,",
     font("bold", 32), INK, anchor="ma")
text(d, (W//2, 920), "not the gun alone on Talmadge's bench.", font("bold", 32), INK, anchor="ma")
footer(d, "7 / 9")
add(im, 11.0)

# =========================================================================
# 7. WRITE IT DOWN  (good vs bad)
# =========================================================================
im, d = canvas()
header(d, "DON'T TRUST YOUR MEMORY", "Write the check down")

prev, total = None, 0

    prev = arr
